name: Johnson's Dictionary
author: Samuel Johnson
description: Sample entries from 'A Dictionary of the English Language' (1755). These definitions are historically documented examples from Johnson's landmark dictionary.

entries.definition: A writer of dictionaries; a harmless drudge, that busies himself in tracing the original, and detailing the signification of words.
A grain, which in England is generally given to horses, but in Scotland supports the people.
One who countenances, supports or protects. Commonly a wretch who supports with insolence, and is paid with flattery.
An allowance made to any one without an equivalent. In England it is generally understood to mean pay given to a state hireling for treason to his country.
A hateful tax levied upon commodities, and adjudged not by the common judges of property, but wretches hired by those to whom excise is paid.
Any thing reticulated or decussated, at equal distances, with interstices between the intersections.
A vain belief of private revelation; a vain confidence of divine favour or communication.
entries.etymology: Greek entheos, possessed by a god
examples: Enthusiasm is founded neither on reason nor divine revelation, but rises from the conceits of a warmed or overweening brain.

entries.definition: The powers of the mind; the mental faculties; the intellect. This is the original signification.
examples: Great wit to madness near allied.

entries.definition: The knee of a horse.
Not exhilarating; not delightful; as, to make dictionaries is dull work.
A small tale, generally of love.
A room on the highest floor of the house.
One who adheres to the ancient constitution of the state, and the apostolical hierarchy of the church of England, opposed to a whig.
The name of a faction.
examples: Whoever has a true value for church and state, should avoid the extremes of whig for the sake of the former, and the extremes of tory on the account of the latter.

entries.definition: A loose sally of the mind; an irregular indigested piece; not a regular and orderly composition.
An assembly of good fellows, meeting under certain conditions.
A convulsion of the lungs, vellicated by some sharp serosity.
Fancy; the power of forming ideal pictures; the power of representing things absent to one's self or others.
examples: Imagination is of three kinds: joined with belief of that which is to come; joined with memory of that which is past; and of things present, or as if they were present.

entries.definition: The protecting or ruling power of men, places, or things; mental power or faculties; disposition of nature by which any one is qualified for some peculiar employment; nature; disposition.
Celebrity; renown; report; rumour.
Expectation of some good; expectation indulged with pleasure.
Dread; horrour; painful apprehension of danger; anxiety.
The passion between the sexes; kindness; goodwill; friendship; fondness; concord.
Moral goodness; efficacy; power; acting power; bravery; valour.

An imaginary being supposed to preside over the material and animal world; the native state or properties of any thing; the constitution of an animated body; disposition of mind; regular course of things; the compass of natural existence; natural affection, or reverence.
The power of doing something not taught by nature and instinct; a science; a trade; artfulness; cunning; skill; dexterity.
Knowledge; certainty grounded on demonstration; art attained by precepts, or built on principles; any art or species of knowledge.
Knowledge natural or moral; hypothesis or system upon which natural effects are explained; reasoning; argumentation; course of sciences read in the schools.
Freedom, as opposed to slavery; freedom, as opposed to necessity; privilege; exemption; permission.
The virtue by which we give to every man what is his due; vindictive retribution; right; rightfulness.
